newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Nomura rates Hungary MOL sell amid fears over rise.
newsitem.headline: Nomura rates Hungary MOL sell amid fears over rise.

text.p: A new report by Nomura Research rates Hungarian Oil and Gas supplier MOL a sell despite improved nine-month results as it fears the government will announce lower-than-expected energy price rises for January.

"Q3 was a little bit better than the last Q3 (in 1995) which obviously is good," Nomura analyst Frances Cloud told Reuters on Tuesday. "But frankly this is irrelevant compared to what's going to be happening on the gas prices."
MOL published January-September results last week which showed a consolidated IAS operating profit of 14.7 billion forints and a pre-tax profit of 11.6 billion forints.

The government is expected to announce on Thursday the amount by which energy suppliers and distributors should be allowed to put up energy prices on January 1. MOL is the exclusive supplier of gas to the distributors.

Western utilities such as French giant Gaz de France and Italgas of Italy bought large stakes in Hungary's energy dicompanies a year ago and were promised an eight-percent return on investment from January 1997.

However, the government put off an October rise until January and appointed a government commissioner, Imre Karl, to review pricing policy after the Hungarian Energy Office recommended a reported 39 percent October rise for electricity and 26 percent for gas.

The postponement provoked fears among the Western investors that the January rise would not be high enough to generate the promised returns and on Wednesday they will hold a final round of negotiations with Karl, privatisation minister Judit Csiha and industry minister Szabolcs Fazakas.
Press reports on Tuesday said Karl was recommending that gas be raised by 16 percent and electricity by 23 percent.
"It is clear that the price increase has become politicised which, if reflected in the final settlement may be to the detriment of the share price performance," the Nomura report said.
Cloud said that even if gas prices do go up by 16 percent MOL may not see such an increase.

"The question is whether it will be 16 percent to end-consumers and say only 10 percent for MOL as they widen the margins for the gas retail companies to please the foreign investors," she said, adding that even if MOL is allowed 16 percent, such a rise was "totally inadequate."

Cloud said the uncertainty was compounded by the lack of a pricing formula which would ensure that future price adjustments would automatically take into account increased costs, inflation and forint devaluation.
"No one in the government ever seems to mention that prices will go up after this price rise," she said.
"If there's no mechanism to hold these prices in real terms then MOL is going to be back where it started. (Prices) are going to be continuously eroded by the devaluation of the forint," Cloud added.
